prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val] Sparse tall row · Server inventory (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Host" · longest unbreakable word 49px · one-line width 65px
  col 2: header "Role" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 3: header "Zone" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 79px
  col 4: header "CPU" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 5: header "Status" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 67px
  col 6: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 64px · one-line width 1403px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"An inventory for checking server identity, function, location, capacity, health and operational notes.","reading":"Readers scan hosts and compare roles, zones, CPU counts and status; the degraded server’s long note calls for closer reading across that row.","groups":["Host and Role identify each server and its function.","Zone and CPU describe placement and capacity for comparison across servers.","Status and Notes pair the health indicator with its operational explanation."],"keep_intact":["Host identifiers and zone names, so servers and locations are easy to distinguish.","CPU values and status words, so comparisons remain quick and unambiguous.","Role names where practical."],"may_wrap":["The long note can wrap at word boundaries; its row is already taller than the others.","Zone names may wrap at natural hyphen boundaries if space is constrained."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[86,80,100,53,88,180],"idea":"Preserve the core inventory values on one line and give the long note room to wrap, accepting substantial horizontal scrolling."},{"name":"B","widths":[70,80,60,53,88,85],"idea":"Use a narrower scrolling table that keeps unbreakable values intact while allowing zone names and the long note to wrap."},{"name":"C","widths":[55,58,55,43,66,82],"idea":"Fit the entire table within the viewport, prioritizing the note and status while accepting broken words and identifiers in narrow columns."}]}
